clue.text: Set a limit on a town's size

blocks.note: to cap something is to set an upper limit on it
the article taken as it stands
a city is a large town

explanation.surface: A council capping how big a town may grow.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'town's size' as one phrase, but the 's is only a link ('is') and 'size' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Capacity is the amount something can hold, its volume or extent, a direct synonym of size.

clue.text: Smiley, perhaps, after Italy's game

indicators.note: one thing coming after another tells you the order in which the pieces are laid down

blocks.note: I is the international vehicle code for Italy
George Smiley is John le Carré's fictional spy; 'perhaps' marks him as one example

explanation.surface: A Smiley, maybe a smiley emoji, following some Italian pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smiley' looks like an emoticon, but it is le Carré's spymaster George Smiley, so it gives SPY once 'perhaps' flags an example.
explanation.definitionFit: I spy is the children's guessing game where players name something seen beginning with a given letter.

clue.text: Proper stuff or malware component?

indicators.note: a component is one part of a larger whole, so the answer is a part of the words beside it

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Asking whether some software is legitimate material or a piece of malicious code.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in stuFF OR MALware; 'Proper' and 'stuff' tempt you to think of real stuff versus malware, but 'component' is the pointer.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal and proper both describe behaviour that follows etiquette and correct convention, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Difficult to keep a ship's bearing, when flustered

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece holds the others inside it

blocks.note: hard means difficult
the article taken as it stands
SS is steamship, as in the SS Great Britain
a compass bearing: E for east

explanation.surface: A navigator struggling to hold a vessel's course while in a fluster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bearing' looks like a course being steered, but it is just a compass point, the usual crossword source for N, S, E or W.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone harassed is worried and hurried by too many demands, the same state as being flustered.

clue.text: Previously in favour of cutting worker's assistance

indicators.note: something cutting through another sits inside it, splitting it in two

blocks.note: the worker bee is the crossword's standard worker
to be for something is to be in favour of it
to give a hand is to give assistance

explanation.surface: Someone who once supported cutting back the help given to workers.
explanation.walkthrough: FOR goes inside BEE, then HAND follows; 'worker' as BEE is a convention worth learning, and the 's only joins it to 'assistance'.
explanation.definitionFit: Beforehand means at an earlier time, in advance, which is what previously expresses.

clue.text: Fruit is one of five issues key at the heart of diets

indicators.note: the heart of something is its centre, so only the central letter is kept

blocks.note: issue means offspring, and a quin is one of quintuplets
C is a musical key
the middle of a five-letter word

explanation.surface: A fruit named as one of five key problems in the diet debate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issues' looks like problems but means children, as in 'died without issue', so one of five is a QUIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The quince is a hard yellow pear-shaped fruit, usually cooked into jelly or paste, an example of the category.

clue.text: One's got to go abroad for Dad's game

blocks.note: Pa is Dad, with its 's kept
a sport is a game

explanation.surface: Someone forced to travel overseas just to catch a match their father follows.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cryptic phrase: 'One's got' means you must have one of these in order to go abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: A passport is the travel document a person must carry to cross borders and enter foreign countries.

clue.text: Favourite drink? Hint — half please!

indicators.note: only half the word survives, so the rest of its letters are dropped

blocks.note: a tip is a hint
the first half of the word, its last three letters dropped

explanation.surface: A regular in a pub hinting at their usual order: a half, please.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half please' reads as ordering half a pint, but it takes half of the word 'please'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone's tipple is the alcoholic drink they habitually prefer, so it means their usual favourite beverage.

clue.text: Broad Street has top notch concert hall

blocks.note: A is the top grade, as in A1 or grade A
a concert hall is one kind of venue

explanation.surface: A particular Broad Street boasting a first-rate concert hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broad Street' looks like a proper name, but it is a lower-case description: a wide street.
explanation.definitionFit: An avenue is typically a wide road, often lined with trees, so a broad street describes it.

clue.text: Oddball's unknown to some

indicators.note: one thing added to another means the pieces simply join up in order

blocks.note: x, y and z are the unknowns in algebra
'any' and 'some' both mean an unspecified amount

explanation.surface: An eccentric whose name means nothing to certain people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unknown to some' reads as 'not known by some people', but it is an algebra letter added to a word for some.
explanation.definitionFit: A zany is an eccentric clownish person, originally a comic stage buffoon, so it names an oddball.

clue.text: Hang about miserably with poor man due to be sacked

indicators.note: a sacked town is ransacked and thrown into disorder, so these letters are thrown about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A penniless man who is about to lose his job drifts around glumly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Due to' looks like the link 'because of', but 'due' is fodder and 'to be sacked' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To mope around is to wander listlessly while feeling sorry for yourself, loitering in low spirits.

clue.text: Drive off with 500 mince pies left

indicators.note: to mince food is to chop it up small, so these letters are chopped and rearranged

blocks.note: D is 500 in Roman numerals
anagram fodder
L for left

explanation.surface: Driving away with five hundred mince pies still uneaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mince pies' is a single Christmas treat on the surface, but 'mince' is a verb telling you to chop up PIES.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispel is to drive away or scatter, as in dispelling doubts or fears, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Indicated Pinot due to be bottled

indicators.note: bottled is slang for drunk, and drunk things stagger out of order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A note that the Pinot Noir is ready to go into bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottled' looks like winemaking, but in British slang it means drunk, hence scrambled; 'due to' belongs to the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To point out is to draw attention to or show, which is what indicated means as a past-tense verb.

clue.text: One hearing story about good man has points to ponder at the end

indicators.note: to go about is to surround, so one piece wraps around another
only the closing letter of the word is kept, the one at its end

blocks.note: a lie is a made-up story
a saint is a good man, abbreviated ST
two compass points, north and east
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A member of an audience hearing a tale about a virtuous man, left with things to think over.
explanation.walkthrough: LIE goes around ST, then N and E (compass points) and R follow; 'good man' as ST (saint) is a standard convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A listener is a person who is paying attention to sound, especially speech, so it names one hearing.

clue.text: Parking in city terrible with a large model

indicators.note: something terrible is in a bad state, so these letters are knocked out of shape
being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: anagram fodder
P is the sign for a car park
the article taken as it stands
L for large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Car parking in a city being awful, and a big fashion model involved somehow.
explanation.walkthrough: CITY is rearranged to TYIC, P is placed inside, then A and L follow. 'Model' is an adjective here, as in a model pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: A model example is a representative one showing the usual features of its kind, which is what typical means.

clue.text: Despite everything, time student put into flat's wasted

indicators.note: wasted is slang for very drunk, so these letters reel out of order
something put into another ends up inside it

blocks.note: anagram fodder
an era is a period of time
L is a learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A student who, against the odds, gets put into a flat that is a wreck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasted' is British slang for drunk, a signal to scramble; 'student' for L comes from the learner plate, and the time and student go in before the scrambled word's last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: After all is an idiom meaning in spite of what was expected or said earlier, matching despite everything.

clue.text: Nowadays church is behind forefront of progress

indicators.note: coming behind something means following it in the order the pieces are laid down

blocks.note: AD, anno Domini, is the present era
the van, short for vanguard, is the forefront
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A complaint that the church lags behind the leading edge of social change today.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forefront of progress' looks like a phrase to take a first letter from, but 'forefront' is VAN and 'progress' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Advance and progress are both nouns or verbs for forward movement or development, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Making sure revolutionary's caught before monarch arrives

indicators.note: coming before means leading, which fixes the order the pieces are laid down

blocks.note: Che Guevara, the crossword's standard revolutionary
c is caught in cricket scoring
a king is a monarch

explanation.surface: Security making certain a rebel is arrested before the king turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: CHE, then C, then KING. 'Caught' as C comes from cricket scorecards, where a batsman dismissed that way is marked c.
explanation.definitionFit: Checking something means verifying or confirming it is correct, the same as making sure of it.

clue.text: Company has European politician contain union's rise

indicators.note: to contain something is to hold it within, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: Co is the abbreviation for company
MEP is a Member of the European Parliament
U for union

explanation.surface: A firm has a Euro MP trying to hold back a trade union's growing power.
explanation.walkthrough: CO, then MEP holding U; the definition 'rise' is a verb here, as a subject might rise or come up.
explanation.definitionFit: To come up is a phrasal verb for moving upward or emerging, as the sun does, a synonym of rise.

indicators.note: a plus sign adds one thing to the next, so pieces join in order
a minus sign subtracts, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: X is ten in Roman numerals
the number two written as a word, less its W
the numeral written as a word

explanation.surface: An algebra sum whose answer is a price of one pound fifty.
explanation.walkthrough: It looks like maths with an unknown x, but x is the Roman ten and '2' is read as a word. 1.50 is a time, not money.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten minutes before two o'clock is the clock time 1.50, written with the British dot between hours and minutes.

clue.text: Prophet put priest on short pilgrimage going north

indicators.note: putting one thing on another stacks them, so they join in order
something short is cut down, so the word loses its final letter
in a down clue, going north means reading upward, backwards

blocks.note: Eli is the priest in the Book of Samuel, a crossword regular
the hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca, here cut to three letters

explanation.surface: A prophet sending a priest on a brief journey northwards.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'on' means placed above, so the priest comes first; the pilgrimage is the hajj, which loses one J before turning upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Elijah is an Old Testament prophet who was taken to heaven in a whirlwind, an example of the category.

clue.text: Force commercial gain from device

blocks.note: g is the symbol for gravitational force
a commercial is an advertisement, an ad
to get something is to gain it

explanation.surface: Pushing to make money out of some invention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial gain' reads as profit, but splits into two pieces: 'commercial' is an advert, 'gain' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A gadget is a small mechanical or electronic tool, so it is a kind of device.

clue.text: Went on for ever about some fungus he discovered

indicators.note: only some of the following words is used, a part rather than the whole

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the third

explanation.surface: A mycologist who talked endlessly about a mushroom he found.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is in funGUS HE Discovered; 'about' links the definition, as you gush about something.
explanation.definitionFit: To gush is to talk with effusive, unrestrained enthusiasm at length, which is going on for ever.

clue.text: Head after more nuts in rough country?

indicators.note: one thing coming after another fixes the order in which the pieces are laid down

blocks.note: nuts means crazy, wild, so more nuts is wilder
a ness is a headland, as in Dungeness, a headland on the Kent coast

explanation.surface: Someone losing their head over nuts growing in some untamed region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' is geographical, a headland (NESS), not a person's head; 'nuts' is an adjective meaning crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: A wilderness is uncultivated, uninhabited land left in its natural state, which is rough country.

clue.text: Aftermath of funeral

definitions.note: a wake is the gathering around a funeral rather than the funeral itself

blocks.note: what follows behind an event, like the trail a ship leaves
the watch or party held for the dead around a burial

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one phrase, the time after a burial, but it splits into two meanings joined by 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: The disturbed water behind a ship gives the idiom in the wake of, meaning consequence; separately a vigil beside the dead.

clue.text: Turn a blind eye to wife's criminal kin!

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so these letters are twisted out of order

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Ignoring the fact that your spouse's relatives are crooks.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition includes 'to': you wink at something to show you will not report it.
explanation.definitionFit: To wink at wrongdoing is an idiom for deliberately overlooking it, the same as pretending not to see.

clue.text: Oddly unable to follow chap's instructions

definitions.note: the answer is singular, a book of instructions

indicators.note: odd-numbered positions are kept, first, third and fifth
following something means coming after it in the order laid down

blocks.note: a chap is a man
its first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: Being strangely incapable of obeying a man's orders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly unable' reads as 'strangely unable' but takes the odd letters; the second piece comes after the first.
explanation.definitionFit: A manual is a handbook that tells you how to operate something, a booklet containing instructions.

clue.text: Expecting working parent to get hold of good nanny, initially

indicators.note: something working is in operation, so the letters are worked into a new order
getting hold of something means gripping it, so one piece holds another
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: anagram fodder
G for good
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A working mum-to-be arranging to hire a good nanny in advance.
explanation.walkthrough: PARENT is rearranged to PRE + ANT, with G and N placed in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Expecting is a gentle idiom for carrying an unborn baby, the state of being with child.
